title: With range-wide GBIF niche indices, North American bird communities followed 4-7% of their spatial temperature gradient in 1970-2025 but 25-30% in 1997-2025; Swedish birds followed 28-53% in 1996-2019
abstract: Question: campaign work found that bird community temperature indices (CTI) follow less than 10-14% of their spatial temperature gradient in time. A butterfly study showed that species temperature indices (STI) from the network's own sites can make non-climatic change look like tracking. Is the bird result an STI artefact? Data: North American Breeding Bird Survey 1970-2025 (126,811 standard runs, 5,308 routes, 413 species), Swedish Bird Survey fixed routes 1996-2019 from BioTIME study 634 (707 routes, 161 species), GHCN_CAMS May-July temperature, and GBIF June occurrence maps (1990-2025) for external breeding-range STIs. Method: CTI with internal (cross-fitted survey-route) STIs or external STIs (four variants), with route x observer effects. Tracking fraction = (CTI trend per C of warming) / spatial CTI slope. 2-degree block bootstrap. Exact split of the internal STI into a range-wide-niche part and a residual. Results: BBS internal and external STIs correlated at 0.95. For 1970-2025 the fraction was 0.14 (0.09-0.19) internal and 0.04-0.08 external (main 0.04, -0.01 to 0.09). The residual carried 75% of the internal CTI trend but only 9% of the spatial slope. It did not predict species trends. A few large-residual species (Canada Goose, Turkey Vulture, Pileated Woodpecker increases) drove it. Late-period internal STIs gave the same 0.15, so range shifts do not explain the gap. With every STI, BBS CTI fell in 1970-1996 while temperature rose, and followed 0.25-0.33 of the gradient in 1997-2025. Responses identified only from temperature variation agreed between STIs: year-to-year anomalies 0.02, between-route warming differences with year effects 0.07-0.09 (intervals include 0). In Sweden the direction reversed: internal 0.30 (0.19-0.49), external 0.53 (0.39-0.75; variants 0.28-0.52). There the residual carried 48% of the spatial slope and 8% of the trend. Conclusion: the STI source changes bird tracking estimates in either direction, so internal-STI fractions need an external check. The long-term 'less than 10%' value mixes a counter-climatic 1970-1996 fall with about 0.3 tracking after 1996 on two continents, near the 0.28 equilibrium fraction of a 75-network lag fit. Limitations: GBIF effort bias and broad species concepts; part of the recent common rise is not shown to follow local warming; period split and year-effect estimators were added after a partial-data look; Sweden has only 24 years.

display.caption: Tracking fraction ((CTI trend per C of warming) / spatial CTI slope) for nine STI versions (blue: internal survey-route STIs; orange: external GBIF June range STIs). Panels: BBS 1970-2025, 1970-1996, 1997-2025, and Swedish fixed routes 1996-2019. 95% intervals from 2-degree block bootstrap. Dashed line: full space-for-time response.

Annual CTI change within route x observer (BBS) or route (Sweden) for the internal STI, the external STI scaled by the fit slope, and the residual part. Internal = intercept + slope x external + residual exactly. In BBS the residual rose steadily while the range-wide-niche part fell to 1997 and then rose.

Internal (survey-route) STI against external (GBIF June breeding range) STI. BBS: 413 species, r = 0.95. Sweden: 161 species, r = 0.72, slope 0.62 (internal STIs compressed). Labelled species have large residuals.
